summary: RFC 7118 defines a WebSocket subprotocol for SIP, and this document updates the SIP Common Log Format from RFC 6873 with a new Transport Flag for SIP over WebSocket. That way logs can show when a SIP message used that transport.

eli5.summary: When a diary records how each message arrived, it needs a letter for each way. This RFC adds a new letter for messages that traveled over WebSocket.

subtitle: A new transport flag value, W, lets SIP Common Log Format records show that a message traveled over WebSocket.

tldr.problem: The SIP Common Log Format from RFC 6873 had Transport Flag values only for UDP, TCP and SCTP, so SIP messages carried over WebSocket (RFC 7118) could not be logged correctly.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines the Transport Flag value 'W' for WebSocket. Plain WebSocket records set the Encryption Flag to 'U' and secure WebSocket (WSS) records set it to 'E'.
tldr.outcome: IANA registered 'W' in the SIP CLF Transport Flag Values registry, and the document updates RFC 6873.

facts.label: Flags Field
facts.value: Five bytes; Transport Flag is the fourth, Encryption Flag the fifth

today: RFC 7355 is an Informational document that updates RFC 6873. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the value W is registered with IANA.

sections.title: Why a New Transport Flag
sections.content:
The WebSocket protocol lets clients and servers exchange messages in both directions over a persistent TCP connection, optionally secured with TLS. RFC 7118 defines a WebSocket subprotocol for carrying SIP messages between a WebSocket client and server.

SIP messages can be logged using the Common Log Format (CLF) from RFC 6873. That format already had Transport Flags for UDP, TCP and SCTP, but none for WebSocket. This document adds one, and so updates RFC 6873.
sections.eli5: A logbook had letters for three kinds of delivery trucks but none for a new kind. This RFC adds the missing letter.

sections.title: Using the WebSocket Transport Flag
sections.content:
In a SIP CLF record, the fourth and fifth bytes of the five-byte Flags Field are the Transport Flag and the Encryption Flag. The values registered before this document were UDP (U), TCP (T) and SCTP (S). This document defines and registers W for WebSocket transport.

Two rules follow, both MUST requirements:

  • Records of messages over a plain WebSocket connection (WS) set the Transport Flag to W and the Encryption Flag to U (Unencrypted).
  • Records of messages over a secure WebSocket connection (WSS, which is WebSocket over TLS) set the Transport Flag to W and the Encryption Flag to E (Encrypted).
sections.eli5: Every log line has two little letters: how the message traveled and whether it was locked. Now W means WebSocket, and the second letter says locked or not.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples, each a SIP INVITE from sip:alice@example.com to sip:bob@example.com with the SDP body left out. The first travels over plain WebSocket, with SIP/2.0/WS in the Via header, and its record begins with the flags RORWU. The second travels over secure WebSocket, with SIP/2.0/WSS, and its record has RORWE.

Each example also gives a bit-exact Base64 version of the log entry and a short Perl script that decodes it. Because of RFC layout limits, records are shown with the <allOneLine/> markup convention from RFC 4475.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows two sample log lines, one for an unlocked WebSocket message and one for a locked one, so you can see the letters in place.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Adding the flag value does not by itself introduce new security considerations. Logging protocol information does raise security, privacy and data protection issues, which RFC 6872 and RFC 6873 describe. Issues specific to WebSocket (RFC 6455) or to SIP over WebSocket (RFC 7118) are left to those documents.

IANA has registered the value W, transport protocol WebSocket, with reference RFC 7118 and RFC 7355, in the SIP CLF Transport Flag Values registry.
sections.eli5: Adding a new letter does not add new dangers, but keeping logs can reveal private things, so be careful with them.
